items.title: Buddhism rejects the existence of a permanent self
items.claim: What is the Buddhist teaching of anatta?

options.text: The soul is eternal and unchanging
There is no permanent, unchanging self (atman); what we call 'self' is a constantly changing aggregation of five skandhas (form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness)
Only the body is real; the soul is illusion

items.reveal:
Anatta (no-self) is one of the three marks of existence in Buddhism, alongside anicca (impermanence) and dukkha (unsatisfactoriness). The doctrine sharply distinguishes Buddhism from Hinduism's atman/Brahman teaching.

The Anattalakkhana Sutta — the Buddha's second sermon — argues each of the five skandhas is impermanent and not under our control, so cannot be 'self'.

Later Mahayana schools developed the concept further. Yogacara introduced 'alaya-vijnana' (storehouse consciousness); some Pure Land traditions speak of 'Buddha-nature' that complicates the picture without abandoning anatta.
items.why: Anatta is one of the most counter-intuitive religious doctrines. It contradicts both Western theological assumptions about the soul and lived experience of continuity — and is the central philosophical claim of Buddhism.

items.title: Pesach commemorates the Exodus from Egypt

options.text: The giving of the Torah at Sinai
The Exodus from Egyptian slavery — the angel of death 'passing over' Jewish homes marked with lamb's blood, the hasty departure (unleavened bread, matzah), the crossing of the Red Sea
The destruction of the Second Temple

items.reveal:
Pesach falls on 15 Nisan (March-April). It lasts 7 days in Israel (and for Reform Jews worldwide), 8 days in the Diaspora for Orthodox and Conservative Jews.

The Seder is the ritual meal on the first night (and second night in the Diaspora). The Haggadah ('the telling') is recited — recounting the Exodus through symbolic foods (matzah, maror, charoset), four cups of wine, and the four questions (asked by the youngest).

The festival ends with 'Next year in Jerusalem'. Its liberation theme has shaped social movements: African American spirituals (Go Down Moses), the Civil Rights movement (King invoked Exodus), Latin American liberation theology.
items.why: Judaism's major festivals carry specific historical content. Pesach is not generic 'spring festival' but structured ritual recreation of a specific liberation narrative — central to Jewish identity for over two millennia.
